## Precision failures and their repair

The original BF16 rectangular failure used B2/H16, 1,023 queries, 17 keys and D128. One dV coordinate was approximately −0.15918 instead of the centered FP64 result −0.18469. Its whole-gradient relative error was only 0.236%, so a norm-only gate missed it. The corrected probability product returns approximately −0.18457 and passes the existing component-wise checks.

A compact cancellation example makes the issue clearer: a single rounded probability operand gives BF16 dV **+0.37109** where FP64 gives **−0.0182377**. FP16 gives **+0.00870514**. A second probability component and its own FP32 accumulator preserve the negative result. Embedding the same finite inputs in square attention demonstrates that rectangular shape is not a mathematical protection.

The corresponding key-gradient failure comes from rounding dS before multiplying by Q. Capturing the actual GPU FP32 dS isolated the loss: its FP64 product with Q agreed closely with the centered reference, while the rounded operand reproduced the released kernel’s wrong-sign result. The low dS product repairs that rounding boundary. An arbitrary query-anchor correction was not substituted for the actual residual product.

High and low products have independent FP32 sums. Interleaving both products into one accumulator was rejected because FP32 accumulation rounding can consume the small residual during cancellation. The low sum is combined only in the epilogue.

An FP16 underflow fixture produces a dV coordinate of about **0.67997**. Unscaled probability components both disappear and produce zero. Scaled residual storage gives about **0.67969**, with all output/dQ/dK/dV gates passing. A short-square variant also fails without scaling. The shared regression factories preserve the exact rounded operands and check these coordinates in addition to whole tensors. The D256 owner retains its separately qualified derivative-packing policy; its probability residual is also scaled.
## Resource choices and rejected controls

The first full-width D128 residual layout was rejected after a severe allocation failure: 40 allocated registers and roughly 3,000 bytes of local memory per thread, with extensive local loads/stores. Its PTX was register-only; the local traffic appeared in assembled SASS. A smaller output fragment removed this spill cliff. This differs from D64’s small, measured spill tradeoff: the final BF16 export has seven local-load and ten local-store sites across the whole function, while FP16 has four and six. These are static sites, not executed counts or runtime percentages. The selected owner still beat the spill-free alternative on complete calls.

A smaller 16-key-row/four-column-warp layout reduced register use substantially but increased complete latency at long D64/D128. The controlled intervention repeats query/gradient staging over more key tiles; lower registers did not establish a speedup. It remains a rejected long-sequence control, while the compact short layout is retained.

Reusing query-column statistics also showed why cold medians are insufficient. FP16 pilot runs favored it by roughly 3–6%, while BF16 often regressed. Four alternating 20-second sustained passes, excluding the first five seconds of each, reduced the aggregate FP16 advantage to about 1.65%. Temperature rose from roughly 55°C to 65°C and sampled board power approached 350 W. The final generic policy keeps the simpler original statistic schedule rather than adding a small dtype-specific preset. Sampled clock values are telemetry, not cycle-normalized timings.

Compute counters were unavailable: a corrected capture attempt returned `ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM`. An earlier export-harness failure is retained separately. Timing, graph identities, deployed code, resources and controlled changes support the conclusions; no cache-hit, stall or utilization percentages were inferred.

The frozen generic correction passed 64 focused cases, including both dtypes, exact key/value/underflow factories, the original rectangular operands, three negative-max key fixtures, signed and zero scales, strided masked GQA and 12 graph replays with changed inputs and poisoned outputs. Separate existing regression methods cover the same public frontends and runtime boundaries. Full GPU discovery passed 194 tests with 56 skips on revision `671a8a2`. The final `2806bcc` runtime then passed all ten shared key/value test methods and a public four-backend dispatch check. These are separate validation runs; the final matrix records its own complete runtime hashes. A later `26a1061` integration check passed eight D64/D128 cases across both dtypes and visibility modes, checking eager outputs/gradients and all three captured phases. Its only runtime differences are the nonselected RTX 5090 schedule and new backward module. The capability guard bypasses that selector on L40S; sixteen direct predicate checks on actual normalized compilation arguments were false, and the new module was never imported.

Twenty focused CPU-FP64-reference cases passed memcheck and racecheck with CUDA API-status reporting suppressed. Unfiltered memcheck reported seven pairs of API-version lookup diagnostics: a 13041 request against driver API 13040 and `cuGetProcAddress_v2` invalid-value status. They were retained separately from kernel-memory findings. Only API-status reporting was suppressed; kernels were not name-filtered. The same memcheck flags detected an intentional invalid global write and returned the configured failure exit code, confirming that memory instrumentation remained active.

`released` is not a claim of a byte-identical historical binary. | Intervention | Observation |

One uninterrupted GPU discovery run on `812aaeb` passed 203 methods in
3591.295 seconds: 129 active passes and 74 hardware/backend skips. It includes
all ten common key/value precision methods, all eight Ti schedule methods,
and tracker, training, graph and compiled-call regressions. Separate actual

key coordinate within 0.70% BF16 and 1.76% FP16 of the closed form, below the
unchanged 2% gate. Broader B2/H4 qualification separately retained 56
rectangular, strided, signed-scale and changed-data checks.

FP16 demonstrates why that resource change alone does not select a preset.
Its S1024 complete pilots improved 4.2% dense and 0.65% causal, but S4096
dense tied and causal regressed 0.74%. FP16 therefore retains the repaired
N1 owner. The BF16 range requires its own public-dispatch, boundary, fallback,
compiled-call, replay and sanitizer qualification; private forced-owner
numbers are selection evidence rather than the final comparison grid.

All 38 strict qualification records passed. Actual resources were 244
registers and 64 KiB for one stage, and 249 registers and 96 KiB for both
two-stage variants, with zero local bytes. Five rotating 100 ms complete
medians were 27.915 ms for the accepted Q64 owner, 29.320 ms for Q32 one
stage, 29.002 ms for Q32 two stages, and 28.894 ms for two stages retaining
upper V. Earlier copies and reduced V reload traffic helped the Q32 control,
but every accepted-Q64 sample beat every variant. All three controls were
rejected; they did not alter the published runtime.

The original bitwise gradient-subset test failed on existing FP32 atomic dQ
order, and its actual operands were retained. Six identical all-gradient calls
varied 46–55 dQ coordinates while the other components stayed identical; maximum
per-head dQ norm error against FP64 remained 0.2993%. All seven subset patterns
launched the same selected kernel symbols and resources. The final tests check
the established per-component norm contract, without a new bitwise guarantee.

The FP32 atomic path also changes cross-block summation order and uses the
architecture's flush-to-zero floating-point reduction instruction. The existing
approximately 1e-21 regression exercises normal FP32 contributions. It does not
qualify FP32 subnormal accumulation. The distinct BF16 diagnostic scales the
sharp-attention dO by approximately 1e-18: production dQ has about 5.05% norm
error and the opaque prototype about 6.23%, both rejected by the 1% gate.
Correctly rounding the FP64 dQ into BF16 has approximately 0.295% error in a
separate CPU representability check. Low-precision operand rounding, tensor
instructions and atomic FTZ all require consideration; these measurements do
not isolate their individual contributions. Subnormal accumulation remains
unqualified and is not hidden inside the normal tiny-gradient pass count.

For each retained case, the harness compares dQ, dK and dV separately with
centered FP64 equations on identical rounded inputs, checks graph replay with
changed dO, and checks changed Q/K/V with freshly computed forward statistics.
It poisons scratch, row statistics, pivots and output storage before replay.
SDPA's own retained-forward backward is measured separately and is never used
as the accuracy oracle. Its failed accuracy cases are diagnostic, not qualified
speedup comparisons.

The frozen opaque configuration passes 13 focused cases covering D64/D128,
FP16/BF16, dense/causal attention, lengths 1/17/65/129/257 and a 4096-token
shifted-key case. These include partial tiles, negative maxima, sharp attention
and the directional cancellation example above. Every accepted case also passes
changed-dO and changed-Q/K/V replay with fresh forward statistics and poisoned
storage. A separate fourteenth subnormal diagnostic is rejected by both CuTe
paths, as detailed above. Selection used seed 1009, qualification seed 1021,
and the seven-round holdout uses seed 1033.

The explicit RTX 4090 entry selects a 128-key backward tile for batch 1, 16 heads, 4,096-token causal D64 attention in FP16/BF16. It retains the 64-key tile at 1,024 tokens: the wider tile regressed that shorter workload. Other head dimensions, dense schedules and fallback boundaries retain their preceding choices. The top-level dispatcher is unchanged.

The initial automatic candidate improved S1024 graph replay but regressed
complete eager calls by about 1–4%. Systems confirmed four tuned launches versus
three generic launches, including gradient preparation and conversion. The
instrumented traces also spent substantial time in kernel-name callbacks, so
their durations were not used as sustained performance estimates.

D128 dense uses a wider key tile to reduce dQ partial updates. Moving V to shared
memory avoids the long-lived register operand that made the earlier M32 layout
spill inside its main loop. The retained layout uses 99,328 shared bytes on the
measured device. D128 causal keeps its M64N64 ownership; the dense D128 layout regressed
causal calls. Long D64 causal uses its independently qualified M64N128 path. D64 causal uses a smaller forward query tile,
which improved the complete call as well as forward latency.

Both backward owners use 64 key/query columns rather than 32. A fused query
centering calculation removes its separate launch. The forward path also skips
padded matrix work. Changing the tile width or padding alone was less effective
than the combined selection. Two- and eight-warp forward alternatives were
slower and were rejected.
### Experiments rejected

Measured interventions also included paired score instructions, smaller N
fragments on long calls, V-register caching, dO-storage reuse, double-buffered Q,
earlier softmax/operand transfers, eight-warp owners, reverse query order,
minimum-residency hints, streamed product operands, and separate QK/dP warp
owners. None provided a reliable complete-call win over the selected policies
for the remaining long D64/D128 gap. Some reduced an isolated phase while
increasing other call costs. Register residency alone was not a consistent gain. Invalid-capacity and setup
failures are recorded separately from correct candidates with slower timings.

Dedicated-loader prototypes used one or two producer warps, two or three
shared-memory slots, and two, three, or four compute warps. The first BF16 layout
showed a roughly 1.3% causal pilot gain, while its dense call was slower.
Subsequent complete-tile and three-compute-warp configurations did not give a
consistent gain across FP16/BF16. Their sampled outputs and gradients passed
FP64 checks; the rejected prototypes did not receive release sanitizer
qualification. The ring uses the SM80-compatible test-wait mechanism described
in the [PTX ISA](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/pdf/ptx_isa_9.2.pdf).

D64 eager performance is near parity with the preceding CuTe path, including a 3.3–3.6% regression in one holdout. Its larger captured-device gain does not become a comparable eager gain: submission and autograd work remain significant. BF16 D128 improves both boundaries. The selected joint calls beat the measured FA2 and SDPA implementations at both boundaries; this does not claim a universal eager improvement over preceding CuTe. Vendor comparisons include their own host wrappers and arithmetic policies.

Earlier seven-window 100 ms runs contained substantial eager variability, including regressions; they remain visible rather than being replaced by the newer protocol. A separate in-process attribution study recorded zero CPU quota-throttling events across 3,888 measured windows and both complete processes. Its instrumented Systems traces show the largest inter-kernel gap between forward and backward preparation in all three compared paths. Neither observation establishes the cause of the earlier variability or a hardware performance ceiling.

The final bounded source passed 84 live-policy cases, nine actual public-frontdoor frames with 18 changed-data/poisoned replays, independent output/dQ/dK/dV and literal-statistic checks, CPU/GPU reference agreement, and actual selected/fallback graph checks. Its frozen CPU tree ran 379 tests total, with 180 skips and no failures; executable hook permissions were restored and checked. All four sanitizer passes and 16 pipeline-code bindings were retained for the unchanged wider GPU implementation. Three final main-kernel bindings, including FP16 D64, passed after narrowing eligibility. Loaded ELF, compiler ELF, PTX/SASS and actual host-library bytes were verified off-host. Public and direct-runner forward, preparation, main and conversion binaries match for both BF16 dimensions.

Actual API qualification passed 12 frontdoor frames, 44 live-metadata/policy cases, 16 changed-data and poisoned-buffer replays, independent O/dQ/dK/dV norm gates and literal saved-statistic checks. Short/partial calls and legacy D64/D128 selection were checked. The frozen tree ran 381 CPU tests total, with 180 skips and no failures. All four sanitizer tools passed on actual selected public calls; reference equations ran on exact CPU copies while implementation kernels remained instrumented. The private geometry comparison separately passed 39 strong fixtures, changed graphs and all four tools for each of three forward controls. Acceptance criteria and rounding remain unchanged.

The complete forward-plus-backward gain over the preceding public G1 path is approximately 4–5% in both boundaries. Larger groups are not a blanket improvement: G4 slightly regressed at S1024, and G4/G16 regressed approximately 4–8% on the S4096 controls. Those negative paired samples remain in the [compact evidence](../results/rtx5090-d256-short-groups.json). The chart also includes held-out dense/long controls whose dispatch is unchanged. Short causal FA2 eager variance is retained; captured comparisons give the more conservative device-path comparison.

G4/G16 each passed 39 strong fixtures, changed/poisoned graphs and all four sanitizer tools before selection. Final actual-public qualification passed 12 API frames, 44 live-policy cases, 16 poisoned replays, independent O/dQ/dK/dV and literal-statistic checks, four sanitizer tools and six strict loaded-code bindings. The frozen CPU run had 391 total tests, 188 skips and no failures. The changed S1024 causal kernel and unchanged S4096 causal control are both bound to loaded ELF/compiler ELF/PTX/SASS, with all 162 raw output files SHA-verified off-host. Backward uses 91,136 shared bytes and 255 registers; local allocation increases from 72 to 96 bytes on the short grouped control, despite the measured latency gain. This does not establish a runtime spill percentage.

After integrating onto current main, three public GPU methods, independent output/dQ/dK/dV and literal-statistic checks, CPU/GPU reference agreement, bounded partial-tile runs under memcheck/racecheck/synccheck/initcheck, the 32-row comparison and two new public-code bindings passed again. The existing long public sanitizer passes were retained for the unchanged backward implementation. Reference equations run on exact CPU copies under sanitizers; GPU kernels, graph replay and poisoned storage remain instrumented. The per-head mathematical norm gates remain 1% for BF16 and 0.5% for FP16, with the existing rounded directed checks. That earlier S4096 integration ran 342 CPU-discovery tests total with 177 GPU/runtime skips and no failures; the final S1024 qualification is recorded above.
Full raw machine captures, source snapshots, failed harnesses and exploratory variants remain outside the tracked tree.

Released is a computation control, not a claim of historical binary identity.
Previous versus CuTe isolates the D16 schedules, D64 ranges and short schedules
in `sm120_schedule.py`. Both retain the current shared precision owners, their
qualified packed-store policy and the compensated normalizer. Released versus
CuTe includes scheduling, ownership and arithmetic changes. A failed numerical row
remains diagnostic and does not establish a qualified speedup.

The public-path regressions cross both sequence axes, the 128/512/4096 range
boundaries and cached rectangular fallbacks. They also check strided, changed
and poisoned graph inputs, signed/zero scales and negative maxima. A causal
closed-form regression shifts the strong key-cancellation query/dO groups by
1031 rows: all active queries see the same original 1031 valid keys, retaining
the exact small negative dK target while exercising the selected long owner.

A deterministic D256 FP16 example initially passed ordinary norm and pointwise
checks but failed the stricter closed-form dK coordinate check. The target is
`-0.001713324311`. The original normalizer and unscaled low operand produce
`-0.001667022705`, a 2.70% error. Scaling the low dS operand alone still leaves
2.15% error.

On the same strong fixture, default SDPA gives dK `-0.177734375` for BF16
and `+0.055694580078` for FP16, against the same negative `-0.001713324311`
reference. Both have 16 dK pointwise failures; their dQ norm errors are 11.69%
and 1.43%, respectively. Actual graph symbols identify the launched native
backend. These are numerical diagnostics, not qualified timing comparisons.
## What the machine code and rejected experiments establish

A private joint prototype reproduced that geometry, shared scores, kept V in
registers and used coalesced opaque FP32 dQ scratch. It was rejected. Before the
new low-component repairs, three rotating 100-ms rounds at BF16 B1/H16/S4096/
D256 gave complete backward times of 6.956 ms for released CuTe, 7.768 ms for
the prototype and 4.599 ms for default SDPA. Separate node-level Systems captures
located 5.747 ms in the joint main loop, 1.928 ms in the centered prepass,
0.078 ms in conversion and 0.031 ms in scratch clearing. Those instrumented
stage means are diagnostics, not the canonical benchmark samples. The prototype
was not qualified against the later low-component cancellation tests and is not
an accuracy-equivalent performance ceiling for a future joint design.

A later fixed forward-owner control kept the current arithmetic, cache policy
and FP16 compensated normalizer, replacing the D256 M64/K16 four-warp TMA
owner with generic M128/K32/eight-warps. At S4096 dense, strict FP64 and changed
storage checks passed, but seven rotating 100-ms rounds showed BF16 forward
1.606→1.762 ms and complete 9.692→9.823 ms; FP16 forward 1.603→1.839 ms and
complete 9.577→9.823 ms. It was rejected. Halving the query-CTA count and its logical KV reads did not
outweigh the complete owner's different copy and compute schedule.

A scalar correction formed by multiplying missing dS mass by an arbitrary
query anchor was tested and rejected. It improves a common-query example but
creates a large new error when that anchor is an unrelated finite outlier hidden
by the mask. The selected low-dS matrix product handles that counterexample.

The entry is currently an experiment. The existing public selector still uses
the qualified Python wrapper; automatic short-call selection needs its own
complete-API comparison. The direct experiment requires the qualified optional
runtime documented in [the A100 schedule](a100-sm80-fa4.md), aligned contiguous
square FP16/BF16 MHA, D64/D128, and positive scales. It propagates unsupported
inputs and execution failures.

The static specialization regressed by 4–6%. Dynamic 32-bit dimensions and
actual stride-divisibility constraints restored the previous GPU performance.
A dynamic variant without the preparation kernel's stride-alignment guarantees
failed compiler IR verification; that failed experiment is retained separately.

Actual graph CUfunction queries report 235 registers for the dynamic D64 main
and 246 for its static control, with equal shared memory and no local storage.
D128 reports 255 registers and 24 local bytes for both forms. Resource counts
alone therefore do not explain the regression. The control retains symbols and
resource metadata; its compiler-artifact requests returned unavailable values.
It does not establish independently captured loaded-image or ISA identity.

The final dynamic GPU methods passed independent per-head output/dQ/dK/dV
checks, literal saved-statistic checks, tails, negative common offsets, rounded
cancellation and underflow fixtures, runtime-scale/cache reuse, and changed
poisoned graphs. Final alignment-guard tests exercise expanded and unaligned
output gradients, rejected unaligned inputs, and selected graph symbols.

Memcheck, racecheck, synccheck and initcheck report zero device errors/hazards
on the tail/changed-graph/alignment smoke set with host API reporting disabled.
The original dynamic memcheck remains explicit: forty host API negotiation
diagnostics, comprising thirteen version-13030 probes and seven version-13041
probes against driver API 13020, plus twenty matching address-lookup failures.
Suppressing those reports does not suppress device checking. The earlier static
metadata run additionally reported unresolved internal-helper lookup diagnostics;
it is not used to qualify the final dynamic entry.

These are constructor defaults and source-derived sequence examples, not captured
activations or checkpoint quality measurements.

| Model sources under `simpletuner/helpers/models` | Default heads / head dimension | Relevant geometry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flux/transformer.py`, `moss_image/transformer.py`, `qwen_image/transformer.py` | 24 / 128 | Matches the D128 cancellation family; the model-head-count test repeats it with H24. FLUX and MOSS concatenate image/text tokens into attention sequences. |

| `sd3/transformer.py` | 18 / 64 | Matches D64; the model-head-count test exercises H18. The 128×128 latent sample and 2×2 patches give 4,096 image tokens; 77 CLIP plus 256 T5 text tokens give a 4,429-token joint example. |

The FLUX packing recipe gives 1,024 image tokens plus 512 text tokens at 512-pixel
square input, and 4,096 plus 512 at 1,024 pixels: joint lengths 1,536 and 4,608.
Those lengths differ from an image-only 1,024/4,096-token benchmark. Variable text,
reference tokens, and masks can also introduce partial tiles.

A packed training sequence contains many query rows; it is not the single-query
reproducer. Packing does not remove the per-row probability reconstruction or
operand-rounding rules. The head/dimension overlaps above establish geometric
relevance, without establishing that a model produces the synthetic cancellation
values. No D512 default is asserted for these constructors.
